name: Tasimelteon

lead: Tasimelteon (Hetlioz) is a melatonin-receptor drug approved in the US for Non-24-Hour Sleep-Wake Disorder, mainly seen in totally blind people, and for nighttime sleep problems in Smith-Magenis syndrome. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed for aligning the sleep-wake cycle, with the hoped-for payoff of clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.

It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors involved in circadian timing, though the label says exactly how it works in Non-24 is unclear. Phase 3 trials in totally blind people reported entrainment of the circadian rhythm in a minority of patients; no research ties it to appearance.

paras: It is taken by mouth at a set time each night under prescription for its approved circadian conditions. It is not a general insomnia pill, and effects on the rhythm build over weeks.
Reported effects include headache, raised liver enzyme ALT, vivid dreams or nightmares and infections. The label warns of somnolence. It is prescription-only.

news.title: Tasimelteon Shows Promise for Delayed Sleep - Wake Phase Disorder

angle.text: Tasimelteon is a prescription circadian-rhythm drug used to align the sleep-wake cycle, discussed on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for Non-24 disorder and Smith-Magenis sleep problems; appearance has not been studied.

lead: Tasimelteon is a prescription melatonin MT1/MT2 receptor agonist developed by Vanda Pharmaceuticals and sold as Hetlioz. The US FDA approved it in January 2014 for Non-24-Hour Sleep-Wake Disorder in adults, and in December 2020 for nighttime sleep disturbances in Smith-Magenis syndrome.[1][2][3]

Its link to appearance is through sleep and recovery: a drug that helps the body clock line up with the day and night aims to give a regular sleep window, and people interested in looking rested, in skin and face quality, and in training recovery treat consistent sleep as a foundation. Published work on tasimelteon itself concerns sleep and circadian outcomes; no study has measured appearance outcomes.

Non-24 is a circadian rhythm disorder mainly affecting totally blind people. Phase 3 trials in totally blind people (SET and RESET) reported entrainment of the circadian rhythm in a proportion of patients on treatment,[4][5] a phase 2/3 programme examined transient insomnia after a shift in sleep time in healthy volunteers,[6] and a 2025 phase 3 trial reported on primary insomnia.[7]

paras: The US label indicates tasimelteon for Non-24-Hour Sleep-Wake Disorder (Non-24) in adults.[2] A later approval covers nighttime sleep disturbance in Smith-Magenis syndrome in patients aged 3 and older.[1] The label states that the mechanism by which it works in Non-24 is unclear but that MT1 and MT2 receptors are thought to be involved in controlling circadian rhythms.[2]

Wikipedia reports that the FDA clarified in October 2014 that the approved use covers both blind and sighted people with Non-24, while the EU approval in July 2015 covered only totally blind adults.[3] Public Citizen had argued that the original label omitted that the studies were in totally blind people.[3]

The most common reactions on the label (above 5 percent and at least twice as frequent as with placebo) were headache, raised alanine aminotransferase, nightmares or unusual dreams, and upper respiratory or urinary tract infection.[2] The label warns of somnolence and advises patients to limit activity after taking it to preparing for bed.[2] A randomized trial examined simulated driving performance in healthy adults after night-time administration.[8] Postmarketing pregnancy reports are insufficient to assess risk, and Wikipedia notes rodent findings at doses above the human dose.[2][3]

Tasimelteon is an agonist at MT1 and MT2 receptors, which are densely expressed in the brain's circadian pacemaker, the suprachiasmatic nucleus.[2][9] It is extensively metabolised in the liver, mainly by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4, and dedicated pharmacokinetic studies examined renal and hepatic impairment, smoking, and interacting drugs.[1][10][11][12][13] An absolute bioavailability study in 14 healthy volunteers compared a capsule with an intravenous infusion.[14]

The compound was known as BMS-214,778 and was first studied for insomnia and other sleep disorders, with phase 3 trials in 2006 and 2008.[3] In 2010 the FDA granted it orphan drug status for Non-24 in totally blind adults.[3] Vanda submitted its New Drug Application in May 2013, and the FDA approved Hetlioz on 31 January 2014, the first approved treatment for Non-24.[3][14] The European Medicines Agency accepted the filing in June 2014 and the EU approval followed in July 2015.[3] In December 2020 the FDA extended the approval to sleep disturbance in Smith-Magenis syndrome.[3]

Tasimelteon is not marketed for appearance. The link people draw runs through sleep: a consistent sleep window supports recovery from training and is associated by many people with a rested look and better skin, so those who focus on sleep as a foundation for looking their best take interest in circadian-rhythm drugs. For people with Non-24 or Smith-Magenis syndrome the prescribed use is to align the sleep-wake cycle with the day-night cycle, and published work measures sleep and circadian outcomes rather than skin or facial appearance.[2][4]

Tasimelteon belongs to the melatonin receptor agonist class, which also includes ramelteon (approved 2005), melatonin as a prescription product (2007) and agomelatine (2009).[3] Reviews of melatonin receptors describe tasimelteon as a high-affinity MT1/MT2 agonist among the most advanced melatonergic drug candidates.[9] Wikipedia lists its formula as C15H19NO2, protein binding of roughly 89 to 90 percent, an elimination half-life of about 0.9 to 1.7 hours, metabolism mainly by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4, and excretion mostly in urine.[3]

Tasimelteon is prescription-only in the United States and the European Union and is sold as Hetlioz (capsules) and Hetlioz LQ (oral suspension). In the US the capsule is indicated for Smith-Magenis sleep disturbance from age 16 and the suspension from age 3 to 15, and the two forms are not interchangeable.[3] Wikipedia reports that rodent studies showed fertility impairment, certain tumours and developmental toxicity at high doses.[3]

A 2026 news report describes a phase 3 trial of tasimelteon in delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, in which the sleep timing of the body clock is shifted later than desired.[15] A small early-phase trial in REM sleep behaviour disorder was terminated.[16]

Two randomised placebo-controlled phase 3 trials, SET and RESET, studied totally blind people with Non-24 and were published in The Lancet in 2015.[4] Earlier phase 2 and phase 3 trials examined transient insomnia after a shift in sleep time in healthy volunteers.[6] A 2025 multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in 322 patients with primary insomnia characterised by difficulty falling asleep used polysomnography over a 5-week treatment interval to examine two tasimelteon doses against placebo.[7] A double-blind randomised trial with an open-label extension studied sleep in Smith-Magenis syndrome.[17]
Further registered trials include phase 1 pharmacokinetic studies and a paediatric study.[10][11][18] No studies were found on tasimelteon for appearance outcomes.
